chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father and Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, altogether from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Sulayman ibn Dawud, from Sufyan ibn Uyayna, from al-Zuhri who said:

I said to Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him): 'Which of the deeds is most superior?' He said: 'The one who alights and departs.' I said: 'And what is the one who alights and departs?' He said: 'Opening the Quran and completing it — every time one comes to its beginning, one travels to its end.'

And he (also) said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Whoever God has given the Quran, and he sees that a man has been given something superior to what he was given, then he has indeed belittled something great and magnified something small.'

key_terms.الْحَالُّ الْمُرْتَحِلُ: The one who alights and departs — a metaphor for continuous, uninterrupted recitation of the Quran from beginning to end and back again
key_terms.فَتْحُ الْقُرْآنِ وَخَتْمُهُ: Opening and completing the Quran — beginning recitation at Al-Fatiha and concluding at Al-Nas, then starting again

ai.seo_question: What does the Imam say is the most superior deed in Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith, transmitted through al-Zuhri from Imam Zayn al-Abidin (AS), addresses the supreme virtue of continuous Quran recitation. The Imam uses the poetic metaphor of a traveller who upon arriving at a destination immediately departs again — describing the one who, upon finishing the Quran, immediately begins it again. The Prophet's appended statement warns that the Quran is among the greatest divine gifts, and anyone who considers anything else superior has committed a grave error of judgement.
